title: TabularBERT: Binning-Based Self-Supervised Learning for Tabular Representation
claim: Continuous values are binned into tokens, embedded with variable and bin information, then trained with masked reconstruction and token prediction.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right, arrows between modules, color-coded embedding grids
description: A wide three-stage pipeline read left to right. Stage 1, Discretization, shows a bimodal density curve with vertical bin boundaries b(1)–b(7). The bin holding a sample x_j is shaded blue and labeled x_j → [bin-3]. Stage 2, Token Embedding, stacks input tokens x1–x4 as rounded boxes ([bin-1], [bin-3], a green-outlined [MASK], [bin-2]). Arrows send them into a yellow Variable Embedding block and a green Bin Embedding block. Each block outputs a colored grid of embedding rows. A grayscale pairwise-distance matrix and a dashed 'Fused penalty' callout link back to the bin embeddings. The two grids merge into one combined heatmap. Stage 3, Masked Self-Supervised Learning, feeds that heatmap into a large blue BERT block. BERT outputs to a Regressor (numerical reconstruction, x̂3) and a Classifier (conditional token modeling, with a bar histogram). Pastel fills dominate, and the eye goes first to the bold stage titles and the central embedding blocks.

abstract: Tabular data is one of the most fundamental and widely used formats for representing structured information. Classical machine learning algorithms continue to achieve substantial success in extracting predictive patterns and constructing accurate models from structured data; however, representation learning approaches that extend language-model-based methods to the tabular setting have opened new opportunities. Nevertheless, conventional tokenization procedures and token embedding mechanisms are not well-suited to numerical variables, as they fail to preserve key numerical properties, including proximity structure and ordinal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TabularBERT, a Transformer-based model that discretizes numerical variables via binning-based tokenization and learns representations that account for numerical proximity and ordinal information while capturing conditional dependencies among variables through masked self-supervised pretraining. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed approach, highlighting the benefits of language-model-based representation learning in the tabular domain.
